A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RIGNO and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–H. Relocated sections and retained visualizations can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original RIGNO benchmark results, scaling experiments, ablations, repeated-seed results, and noise-robustness analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, distribution-shift tests, transfer-learning experiments, and computational benchmarks.

M1.justification: The regional graph construction, encoder–processor–decoder architecture, edge masking, time conditioning, all2all loss, and fractional pairing remain unchanged. Detailed architecture equations move to Appendix B; new model configurations and transfer-learning experiments do not establish a revision to the proposed method.

E1.justification: The original benchmark datasets are retained, and Poisson-Gauss adds an elliptic task on point clouds and Cartesian grids. Appendix F.8 additionally evaluates Darcy Flow, Smooth Transport, and Compressible Euler under shifts in characteristic length scales, perturbation locations, and airfoil geometry complexity, substantially broadening task and test-condition coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds MeshGraphNet and UPT to the point-cloud comparisons that previously contained Geo-FNO, FNO DSE, and GINO. Appendix G.8 adds Transolver comparisons on five datasets, while Appendix F.10 compares additional GINO configurations. The Cartesian-grid comparator set remains CNO, scOT, and FNO.

E3.justification: Figure 3b changes from training at 2Δt intervals through t14 with Δt rollouts to training at 4Δt intervals through t16 with AR-4 inference. The spatial ablation changes from 92² training resolution, although v2 inconsistently reports 42² in the text and plot versus 64² in the caption. New OOD, transfer, and computational experiments introduce additional sampling, normalization, training, and benchmarking protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds regional-node-count ablations, MeshGraphNet resolution tests, OOD robustness tests, transfer-learning analyses, and accuracy–cost comparisons in Appendix F. It also revises the main spatial and fractional-pairing ablations. Existing model-size, noise-robustness, and uncertainty analyses are largely retained after relocation.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-seed mean and standard deviation results for NS-PwC and NS-SVS, single-seed training elsewhere, and uncertainty visualizations from 20 stochastic rollouts. No new statistical reporting procedure is introduced. The reassignment of the two seed-result entries changes results, not the uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Matched scores from v1 Table 1 remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial benchmark, OOD, transfer, and resource results. For example, Cartesian Poisson-Gauss gives scOT 0.68% versus RIGNO-18's 1.80%. The seed table changes NS-PwC from 1.05 ± 0.040% to 2.50 ± 0.157%, with NS-SVS changing conversely. Figures 3a–b report replacement results under changed settings, and the 10Δt curve is removed from the lead-time analysis.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds the formal Poisson problem and its Gaussian-source distribution. The existing solution-operator definitions, architecture equations, and loss mathematics are retained or relocated. Neither version provides a RIGNO approximation theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The central claims of accurate, resolution-flexible graph-based operator learning remain. v2 additionally claims that edge masking improves optimization and accuracy, whereas v1 discusses an accuracy tradeoff. Cartesian benchmark dominance is qualified from winning every tested dataset to winning eight of nine.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations involving weaker spatial correlations, local versus global interactions, weaker advantages on elliptic problems, OOD failure mechanisms, and computational tradeoffs. It interprets Smooth Transport's deterioration as sensitivity to non-local shifts. Conversely, v1 Appendix B.2's explicit limitation concerning more general boundary conditions is removed, and the 3D limitation no longer mentions computational cost.

D1.justification: v2 documents the MeshGraphNet implementation, UPT configurations and training settings, and Transolver size constraints. It newly discloses tuning on one internal dataset, RTX 3090 hardware, and an estimated 9,000 GPU hours for RIGNO experiments. Existing RIGNO defaults and the code link remain, but the direct dataset DOI link in v1's bibliography disappears.

R1.justification: The introduction and new related-work discussion substantially expand comparisons with MeshGraphNet, multiscale graph methods, GINO, UPT, and neural-field approaches. New citations include Multiscale MeshGraphNets, two neural-field works, and Transolver. v2 also more explicitly credits prior time conditioning and distinguishes fractional pairing from earlier fixed-step output recycling.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the introduction and edge-masking explanation, adds an explicit contribution list, and condenses the main architecture description by moving equations to Appendix B. Boundary-condition material is reorganized into Appendix A, experimental analyses and baseline appendices exchange order, and related work and limitations receive separate headings.

P2.justification: The original combined benchmark table becomes Tables 1 and 2, with additional rows and comparator columns. Scaling and ablation plots are substantially reformatted, and new regional-node, OOD, computational, Transolver, transfer, and Poisson displays are added. Existing architecture and most solution visualizations are retained but resized or relocated within the revised conference layout.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical support for the unchanged method: direct graph and attention comparisons address important omissions in v1, while OOD tests expose failure conditions and transfer and resource studies clarify practical usefulness. Expanded implementation details improve assessability. These gains outweigh localized reporting defects, notably Figure 3a's conflicting training resolutions and Appendix F.10's claim of consistently superior accuracy despite GINO outperforming RIGNO on Elasticity in Table F.4. Removal of the boundary-condition caveat and dataset link remains a drawback.
